summary:
Kwara stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the federal criminal law apply in the state, and no Kwara-specific statute on same-sex conduct or gender identity is documented in the sources assembled for this record. In 2022 a court ruled sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the act unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, and that ruling applies in Kwara.

Kwara is not among the twelve states that adopted sharia penal law: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. No sharia penal application is documented for Ilorin or anywhere else in the state, and the death-penalty exposure under state Zina provisions recorded in those twelve states does not extend to a visitor here.

No Kwara-specific arrest, prosecution, raid or act of violence against a trans or gender-nonconforming person appears in the sources covering this state. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the 2014 act, which records mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions across Nigeria, names no case in Kwara. That silence marks the limit of what these sources cover; it is not evidence that enforcement or violence is absent in the state.
tangentialFactors:
The statute applied in Kwara has produced documented enforcement elsewhere in Nigeria, and a visitor should expect the same legal exposure. Police operations against private gatherings and hotels have yielded mass arrests in other jurisdictions: more than 100 people at a hotel party in Asaba in June 2018, 57 young men at a Lagos hotel in August 2018, 67 people in Warri in August 2023 and 76 people at a party in Gombe in October 2023. These are raw counts from named operations, not per-capita figures; they show where raids occurred, not comparative risk between states.

Two further national patterns are recorded in the parent material and are not tied to any one state: 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ people through dating applications to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed under threat of outing, documented in April 2024, and proposals to criminalise cross-dressing reported in September 2022, which met fear among transgender Nigerians. No equivalent legislative proposal or gang operation is documented specifically in Kwara.

The killing of the transgender TikToker known as 'Abuja Area Mama', whose beaten body was found on a highway in August 2024 with no suspect charged six months later, occurred in Abuja and not in Kwara. It is recorded here only as a comparison point for how a trans-specific killing has been handled elsewhere under the same national framework.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kwara live under the federal criminal law and the 2014 act, with no state-level decriminalisation, anti-discrimination statute or gender-recognition provision documented in these sources. The 2022 court ruling striking sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the act as unconstitutional and unenforceable is available to residents on the same terms as to anyone else in the country.

Criminal matters in Kwara proceed through the secular courts; the state has no sharia penal courts and no documented sharia penal application in Ilorin or elsewhere. No state-level protection machinery, hate-crime provision, or complaint route for LGBT residents in Kwara is identified in the sources covering this record.

Police conduct in Kwara is not documented in these sources. The extortion and arbitrary-arrest practices recorded against police elsewhere in Nigeria under the 2014 act, including a March 2025 case in which a man was struck with a police gun and released after paying part of a demanded bribe because he 'looked gay', are not evidenced here as Kwara practice.
